rationale: The entry identifies “the life” specifically as law-shaped covenant existence. Deuteronomy 30 and Leviticus 18 establish a genuine covenantal use of “life,” closely associated with obedience, blessing, continued possession of the land, and attachment to God. They do not, however, establish that this is the controlling meaning of “the life” in John 14:6. Matthew 7:14 also distinguishes the way from the life to which it leads, rather than defining life as the act of walking that way. The strongest alternative—divine and eternal life embodied in and imparted through Christ—fits Jesus’ personal identification as “the life,” the way/life distinction, and the resurrection context of John 11:25 more directly. The book can accommodate those details only by adding the disputed premise that Christ is embodied Torah and that covenant conduct itself constitutes the life. Thus the covenantal reading is an important background register, but not the best overall identification of the term.
book_secondary_elaborations: This existence is lived by walking in “the Way.”
This walk is governed by God’s law.
unsupported_glossary_assertions: That covenant existence, rather than divine or eternal life in Christ, is the defining referent of “the life.”
That “the life” itself is the life lived while walking in the Way; Matthew 7:14 instead presents the way as leading to life.
chapter_only_objections: The exclusive reduction of “the truth” to God’s law is not established by the glossary entry’s evidence.
The equation of light with visible law-observance is asserted through a separate symbolic derivation rather than demonstrated here.
The identification of the tree of life as the covenant nation goes beyond the glossary entry and is not required by Proverbs 3:18.
The claim that Genesis 3:24 preserves rather than bars access to the tree of life is difficult to reconcile with Genesis 3:22-24 as a whole.
Identifying Eden’s flaming sword specifically with the word of God depends on a cross-context symbolic equation rather than an explicit textual identification.
The highway, wedding-garment, doorway, and Passover-post constructions are broader typological arguments absent from the glossary entry.
The claim that Jesus is “the Torah embodied” is a chapter-level theological conclusion, not an assertion printed in the glossary entry.
strongest_counter_interpretation: “The life” is divine and eternal life—present communion with God and future resurrection life—personally embodied in Jesus and bestowed through him. Covenant obedience describes one manifestation or antecedent of that life, not its exhaustive definition.
counter_core_identification: “The life” is eternal divine life embodied in and mediated by Christ.
material_core_denial: The covenant-obedience passages do not warrant identifying law-shaped covenant existence itself as the referent of Jesus’ title “the life”; they describe covenant conditions, blessings, or manifestations of life whose ultimate source is God and, in Johannine usage, Christ.
counter_case: John 14:6 grammatically identifies Jesus himself as “the life,” favoring a personal and christological referent rather than merely a mode of lawful existence.
John 11:25 joins “the resurrection” and “the life” and promises life to one who dies, directly supporting resurrection and eternal life mediated by Christ.
John 1:4 and 1 John 5:11-12 locate life in the Son and portray possession of the Son as possession of life.
John 17:3 describes eternal life relationally as knowing the Father and Jesus Christ, not simply as Torah-shaped conduct.

Matthew 7:14 distinguishes the way from its destination: the way leads to life. This is more naturally explained if faithful conduct leads to divine or eschatological life rather than being identical with it.

Deuteronomy 30:20 says that the LORD himself is Israel’s life. Obedience and covenant attachment are integral to the context, but the verse locates life ultimately in God rather than defining it merely as compliant conduct.
Leviticus 18:5 supports a covenantal life-obedience relationship, but it does not by itself decide the christological meaning of “the life” in John.
book_explanatory_advantages: It takes seriously the strong association between life, obedience, covenant blessing, and land in Deuteronomy 30.
It gives Leviticus 18:5 a straightforward role in explaining why Scripture can connect keeping God’s statutes with living.
It recognizes that Matthew 7:14 places life at the end of a morally demanding way rather than presenting life as detached from conduct.
It offers an Old Testament covenant background for the Johannine title instead of treating John 14:6 in isolation.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It directly explains why Jesus can personally say, “I am … the life.”
It integrates present spiritual life, relationship with God, and future resurrection without reducing any of them to legal conduct.
It preserves Matthew 7:14’s distinction between the way and the life to which that way leads.
It explains John 11:25’s association of life with resurrection and life after death.
It accounts for texts locating life “in” the Son and making Christ its source and embodiment.
It can incorporate Deuteronomic covenant obedience as an antecedent or expression of communion with God without making it the exhaustive meaning of every definite use of “the life.”
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Matthew 7:14’s explicit distinction between the way and the life to which it leads conflicts with defining life itself as the walking of that way.
John 11:25-26 presents Jesus as resurrection and life for one who dies and then lives through belief in him; law-shaped covenant conduct alone does not explain this resurrection function.
The Johannine formulation that life is in the Son and possessed by having the Son is more naturally personal and participatory than a definition of life as covenant conduct.
unresolved_objections: The covenantal interpretation remains a substantial Old Testament component of the biblical theology of life.
Divine life in Christ is not morally detached from obedience, so the two readings overlap in application even though they differ in primary identification.
The definite expression “the life” is context-sensitive, and no single formula necessarily exhausts every biblical occurrence.
